title: Market Equilibrium & Imperfect Competition
sub: Topics 7–8 · lecture of 10 Nov · equilibrium, surplus, state interventions, imperfect markets
blurb: Why the market settles at Qd = Qs, consumer and producer surplus, what shifts the equilibrium, price ceilings and floors, and what changes when a firm can set its own price.
h1: Market equilibrium and the step to imperfect competition
lede: First the whole market: where supply meets demand, who gains from trading (consumer and producer surplus), and what happens when curves shift or the state fixes the price. Then the big switch: firms that can affect the price, where MR falls below the price and some surplus is lost.
six: **Market equilibrium**: Qd = Qs. Above it there is a **surplus** that pushes the price down, below it a **shortage** that pushes the price up.
**Consumer surplus** = TU − real expenditure. **Producer surplus** = Σ(P − MC) = TR − VC. Perfect competition is **allocatively efficient**: MU = MC.
Both curves shift: **ΔS > ΔD → P falls**, **ΔD > ΔS → P rises**. Steep (inelastic) demand: P moves a lot, Q a little.
**Price ceiling** below equilibrium → shortage (regulated rents). **Price floor** above equilibrium → surplus (subsidised farm prices).
Imperfect competition: at least one seller can affect the price, demand d slopes down, **MR < P**. Same rules: π = TR − TC and **MR = MC**.
Because **P > MC** there is a **deadweight loss** (allocative inefficiency). Monopoly power: **Lerner index L = (P − MC) / P**.
must: Equilibrium and surplus; ceiling and floor; MR < P, Lerner index and deadweight loss
foot: Source: 3BE123 lecture slides of week 8 (Perfect Competition: completion; Imperfectly Competitive Market), Ing. Z. Dzbánková, VŠE.

questions.q: What is market equilibrium?
questions.answer: The price at which the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied
wrong: The price at which every firm makes a profit
The highest price buyers are willing to pay
The price set by the state
questions.e: Graphically the intersection of the supply and demand curves. The equilibrium price is a compromise between buyers and sellers.

questions.q: Sellers try to sell above the equilibrium price. What happens?
questions.answer: A surplus appears and the price falls
wrong: A shortage appears and the price rises
questions.e: Above P*, Qs > Qd: unsold goods. Sellers lower the price back towards equilibrium.

questions.q: Buyers want to pay less than the equilibrium price. What happens?
questions.answer: A shortage appears and the price rises
wrong: A surplus appears and the price falls
questions.e: Below P*, Qd > Qs: not enough goods. Buyers compete and the price goes up.

questions.q: What is the condition for allocative efficiency in the lecture?
questions.answer: MU = MC
questions.e: The value of the last unit to the consumer (MU) equals the cost of making it (MC). Perfect competition reaches this because P = MU and P = MC.

questions.q: How is consumer surplus defined?
questions.answer: Total utility minus real expenditure
questions.e: CS = TU − what the consumer really pays. In the graph: the area under demand and above the price.

questions.q: How is producer surplus defined?
questions.answer: The sum of price minus marginal cost over all units sold (= TR − VC)
questions.e: PS = Σ(P − MC). In the lecture example P = 10 gives Q = 5 and PS = 5 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 0 = 11 = TR − VC = 50 − 39.

questions.q: Lecture example: VC for Q = 1…5 is 5, 12, 20, 29, 39 and P = 10. What is the producer surplus?
Supply and demand both increase, but supply increases more (ΔS > ΔD). What happens to the price?
questions.answer: The price falls
questions.e: Lecture rule: ΔS > ΔD → P falls; ΔD > ΔS → P rises. The quantity rises in both cases.

questions.q: Supply falls and demand is very inelastic (steep). What mainly changes?
questions.answer: The price rises a lot, the quantity hardly changes
wrong: The quantity falls a lot, the price hardly changes
questions.e: With inelastic demand people keep buying almost the same amount, so the adjustment happens through the price. With elastic demand it is the quantity that changes more.

questions.q: In the very short run, what does the supply curve look like?
questions.answer: Vertical: the quantity cannot change yet
wrong: The same as in the long run
questions.e: In the very short run supply is fixed (e.g. today's fish catch). A demand increase only raises the price. Over the short and long run supply becomes flatter (more elastic).

questions.q: What does a price ceiling below the equilibrium price cause?
questions.answer: A shortage (Qd > Qs)
questions.e: Maximum price below P*: buyers want more, sellers offer less. Example: regulated rents.

questions.q: What does a price floor above the equilibrium price cause?
questions.answer: A surplus (overproduction)
questions.e: Minimum price above P*: Qs > Qd. Example: subsidised prices of agricultural produce.

questions.q: The state puts an excise tax (duty) on a good. What happens in the market?
questions.answer: Supply shifts up by the tax, the price buyers pay rises and the quantity falls
wrong: Demand shifts to the right and the quantity rises
The price buyers pay falls by the whole tax
Nothing changes, sellers pay it from their profit
questions.e: The tax raises sellers' costs per unit: supply shifts up. Buyers pay more, sellers keep less, less is traded. Who carries more of the tax depends on elasticity.

questions.q: What is the key feature of imperfect competition?
questions.answer: At least one seller can affect the price
wrong: There are no barriers to entry
questions.e: The firm is not a price-taker. To sell more it has to lower the price, so it faces a downward-sloping demand curve d.

questions.q: Which are the three forms of imperfect competition in the lecture?
questions.answer: Monopoly, oligopoly, monopolistic competition
questions.e: The lecture lists monopoly, oligopoly and monopolistic competition.

questions.q: Which is NOT a reason for imperfect competition in the lecture?
questions.answer: A homogeneous product sold by many small firms
wrong: Exclusive ownership of a key resource
questions.e: That describes perfect competition. Reasons for imperfect competition: cost conditions, barriers, differentiation, legal restrictions, asymmetric information, state intervention, politics, exclusive ownership of a key resource.

questions.q: Which is the SAME in perfect and imperfect competition?
questions.answer: Profit is maximised where MR = MC
wrong: The demand curve of the firm is horizontal
The firm has a supply curve
questions.e: Identical features: π = TR − TC, MR = MC, the cost curves, and AR = P = d.

questions.q: In imperfect competition, how does MR compare with the price?
questions.answer: MR is lower than the price
wrong: MR is higher than the price
questions.e: To sell one more unit the firm must cut the price on all units, so the extra revenue is less than the price. For P = a − bQ, MR = a − 2bQ.

questions.q: What does the Lerner index L = (P − MC) / P measure?
questions.answer: Monopoly power: how far the price is above marginal cost
questions.e: L is between 0 and 1. In perfect competition P = MC, so L = 0. The higher L, the more market power.

questions.q: Why is there a deadweight loss in imperfect competition?
questions.answer: Because P > MC, less is produced than is efficient
wrong: Because the firm makes a loss
questions.e: Units that buyers value above their cost are not produced. That lost surplus is the deadweight loss = allocative inefficiency.

questions.q: On a straight downward-sloping demand line, where is total revenue at its maximum?
questions.answer: Where demand is unit elastic (|E| = 1) and MR = 0
wrong: Where MR is at its maximum
questions.e: In the elastic part (|E| > 1) MR > 0 and TR rises with Q. In the inelastic part MR < 0 and TR falls. The top of the TR hill is at |E| = 1.

questions.q: Why does an imperfectly competitive firm have no supply curve?
questions.answer: The relationship between price and quantity is ambiguous: the same Q can go with different prices
wrong: Because its MC curve is horizontal
Because the state sets its quantity
questions.e: The firm chooses Q (MR = MC) and then the price from its demand curve. Different demand curves can give the same Q at different prices.

questions.q: If an imperfectly competitive firm earns only a normal profit, where is its output?
questions.answer: Before (to the left of) the minimum of AC
wrong: Exactly at the minimum of AC
questions.e: Its demand curve slopes down, so it touches AC on AC's falling part. In perfect competition normal profit is at Q = min AC.

vocab.meaning: The situation where the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied (Qd = Qs) at an acceptable price for both sides.
Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded (price above equilibrium). Pushes the price down.
Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied (price below equilibrium). Pushes the price up.
Resources make what people value most: MU = MC, the total surplus is as large as possible.
Total utility minus real expenditure: what buyers would pay minus what they pay.
The sum of price minus marginal cost over every unit sold; equals TR − VC.
A maximum price set below equilibrium. Causes a shortage. Example: regulated rents.
A minimum price set above equilibrium. Causes a surplus. Example: subsidised farm prices.
A tax (duty) per unit sold. Shifts supply up, raises the buyers' price, lowers the quantity.
A market where at least one seller can affect the price; the firm's demand slopes down.
One seller of a product with no close substitutes.
A few large sellers who watch and react to each other.
Many sellers of differentiated products, each with a little power over its price.
Products are made different (brand, quality, design), so buyers do not see them as identical.
Measure of monopoly power: L = (P − MC) / P, between 0 and 1.
Total surplus lost because less is produced than is efficient (P > MC).

facts: At the market equilibrium the quantity demanded equals the quantity {supplied|produced last year|imported|wanted by the state}.
A price above equilibrium creates a {surplus|shortage|tax|ceiling}.
Allocative efficiency means marginal utility equals marginal {cost|revenue|product|utility}.
Consumer surplus equals total utility minus real {expenditure|revenue|cost|income}.
Producer surplus is the sum of price minus {marginal cost|average cost|fixed cost|marginal utility}.
If supply grows more than demand, the price {falls|rises|stays|doubles}.
In the very short run the supply curve is {vertical|horizontal|downward sloping|U-shaped}.
A binding price ceiling causes a {shortage|surplus|tax|subsidy}.
Subsidised prices of agricultural produce are an example of a price {floor|ceiling|tax|index}.
In imperfect competition at least one seller can affect the {price|weather|technology|population}.
In imperfect competition marginal revenue is {lower|higher|equal|unrelated} than the price.
Price above marginal cost causes a {deadweight loss|consumer gain|surplus of goods|shortage of labour}.
sheet: MR = MC, then P from d (P > MC)
